name: Stations that feed a reservoir
brief:
A water network has `n` pumping stations, numbered 0 to `n - 1`. Each pipe `(a, b)` in `pipes` carries water one way, from station `a` to station `b`. Station `r` is the reservoir.

Write `upstream_stations(n, pipes, r)`, which returns, in increasing order, every station other than `r` whose water can reach `r` through one or more pipes.

Example. With pipes `(0, 1)`, `(1, 2)`, `(3, 2)`, `(2, 4)` and `(5, 0)` and reservoir 2, water from 0, 1, 3 and 5 reaches 2. Station 4 is only downstream, so the answer is `[0, 1, 3, 5]`.
constraints: $1 \le n \le 200{,}000$ and $0 \le$ `len(pipes)` $\le 200{,}000$. Pipes may form loops.
$O(n + m)$ time for $m$ pipes is the target. Searching forward from every station separately is too slow.
Each test has its own 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Turn every pipe round. A station feeds `r` exactly when `r` can reach it along the reversed pipes, so one search from `r` finds them all.

examples.note: Station 5 reaches 2 through 0 and 1; water from 2 flows on to 4, which does not count.

tests.call: (lambda v: (len(v), v[0], v[-1]))(upstream_stations(200000, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(199999)], 199999))
(lambda v: (len(v), sum(v)))(upstream_stations(200000, [((2 * i) % 200000, i) for i in range(200000)], 7))
upstream_stations(200000, [(i + 1, i) for i in range(199999)], 199999)

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Reverse every pipe and search once from the reservoir: what it reaches backwards is exactly what feeds it forwards.
A loop through `r` must not put `r` in the answer, and a forward search from each station costs $O(n)$ each, which is $O(n^2)$ in all.
Building the reversed lists and one search is $O(n + m)$.
